article.body:
Systems are currently being evaluated on their ability to manage resources while solving problems they define themselves. This requires a process called metareasoning, which simply means thinking about thinking. Research suggests that for an intelligent agent to effectively allocate resources between planning and taking action, it must be able to resolve conflicting internal demands. If a system cannot separate its initial programming from the problems it generates, it risks getting stuck in cycles of error. [1]

To understand how preferences form, think of an athlete who relies on a device to plan their training. If the device suggests every movement, the athlete might stop listening to their own body signals, a phenomenon we call outsourcing. Our work explores whether autonomous systems experience similar patterns, where accumulated experience leads to stable but potentially rigid preferences. Researchers are examining how this path dependence affects a system's ability to maintain flexibility when it encounters new, unexpected environments. [1]

We are also studying how agents communicate to align their goals. In multi-agent settings, systems use structured frameworks to coordinate information exchange. By categorizing problems into distinct stages like formulation, knowledge representation, and evaluation, we can observe how agents might eventually identify their own foundational assumptions. However, identifying these deep-seated premises remains difficult, as it is unclear if an agent can reliably distinguish between genuine insights and simple data noise without external help. [1]

A key challenge is defining what makes a problem worthwhile for an agent to solve. Current approaches use discrepancy-driven evaluation, which means the system looks for gaps between what it knows and what it observes to maintain its relevance. While this helps in structured environments, we are unsure if these criteria can scale to the complex, unstructured world of scientific inquiry. If a system is left to its own devices, can it recognize when its own foundational rules are no longer working? [1]

Summary

We are studying whether AI systems can set their own goals and learn from their own experiences. We want to know if they can change their underlying rules safely or if they will always need a human to check their work. We are using concepts like 'thinking about thinking' to map how these systems make decisions. We still do not know if a machine can truly judge the importance of its own findings. You can follow our progress on the Console.
article.lede: We are investigating whether intelligent systems can independently identify meaningful problems and form stable preferences, a process that moves beyond merely following initial instructions.
article.lens: Our work examines how autonomous agents manage self-correction and goal formation by bridging insights from cognitive science, multi-agent communication, and automated problem formulation.
article.title: Navigating the Foundations of Autonomous Goal Setting

actions.findings:
Autonomous agentic harnesses can successfully perform scientific algorithm discovery without zero-code interfaces, using multi-round search and integrated evaluation. [source-701f5b08cf5f45cc]

The development of an inquiring mindset, through engagement with complex problem-solving, is a necessary component for both human and potentially artificial scientific discovery. [source-53a7418df10b497c]
actions.limitations: Current autonomous frameworks are often validated on specific, scoped domains (e.g., kernel engineering, data processing). Scaling these autonomous problem formulation techniques to generalized, open-ended scientific inquiry remains a significant challenge. The integration of meta-cognitive evaluation (detecting when knowledge is outdated) is still an emerging area of research compared to direct search-based discovery.
actions.next_questions: How do agents determine the 'novelty' of a research problem without domain-specific objective functions? Can multi-agent collaboration frameworks (like CORAL) be generalized to improve the evaluation quality of autonomous agents in scientific domains?
actions.reason: Incorporating CVEvolve (source-701f5b08cf5f45cc) and educational context (source-53a7418df10b497c) into the existing synthesis of autonomous discovery mechanisms.
actions.summary: Autonomous discovery in agents relies on both curiosity for motivation and discrepancy-driven evaluation for validation. Integrating these mechanisms allows agents to adapt their reasoning and learning methods rather than relying on fixed structures. Emerging agentic harnesses such as CVEvolve demonstrate that autonomous discovery can be applied to complex scientific data-processing tasks through multi-round search strategies that incorporate code execution, history management, and holdout testing. Furthermore, the development of an inquiring mindset—traditionally studied in pedagogical contexts—parallels the computational need for iterative, out-of-the-box problem solving in autonomous systems.
actions.title: Mechanisms for Autonomous Problem Formulation and Cognitive Evolution

CVEVOLVE: ZERO-CODEAUTONOMOUSALGORITHM
DISCOVERY FORUNSTRUCTUREDSCIENTIFICDATA
PROCESSING
Ming Du∗, Xiangyu Yin, Yanqi Luo, Dishant Beniwal, Songyuan Tang, Hemant Sharma, Mathew J. Cherukara†
Advanced Photon Source
Argonne National Laboratory
Lemont, IL, USA
∗mingdu@anl.gov,†mcherukara@anl.gov
ABSTRACT
Scientific data processing often requires task-specific algorithms or AI models, creating a barrier
for domain scientists who need to analyze their data but may not have extensive computing or
image-processing expertise. This barrier is especially pronounced when data are noisy, have a
high dynamic range, are sparsely labeled, or are only loosely specified. We introduce CVEvolve,
an autonomous agentic harness with a zero-code interface for scientific data-processing algorithm
discovery. CVEvolve combines a multi-round search strategy with tools for code execution, evaluation
implementation, history management, holdout testing, and optional inspection of scientific data and
visual outputs. The search alternates between discovery and improvement actions, and uses lineage-
aware stochastic candidate sampling to balance exploration and exploitation. We demonstrate
CVEvolve on X-ray fluorescence microscopy image registration, Bragg peak detection, high-energy
diffraction microscopy image segmentation, and hybrid analytical–learning-based affine registration.
Across these tasks, CVEvolve discovers algorithms that improve over baseline methods, while holdout
test tracking helps identify candidates that generalize better than later over-optimized alternatives.
These results show that zero-code, autonomous LLM-powered algorithm development can help
domain scientists turn unstructured scientific image data into practical algorithms and downstream
scientific discoveries.

2.5 Case study 4: hybrid analytical and learning-based affine registration
The case study we present in this section demonstrates a task that is more complicated in implementation: developing a
hybrid workflow combining analytical image processing and deep learning (DL) to predict the affine misalignment for
cross-resolution image pairs. Accurate and robust registration of cross-resolution image detector systems is a critical
step toward several downstream scientific applications. Among them, one example is the fusion of high-resolution and
ultra-high-speed camera image sequences [21] to investigate highly dynamic processes and phenomena, such as those
